personalInfo.detailedBio: Senior Frontend Engineer with 7+ years building React and TypeScript products for enterprise SaaS, working at SwiftConnect in Montréal from Nov 2020 through March 2026. Built the Node.js and React SDKs used by the front-end team and third-party customers, a Storybook-backed component library with WCAG AA accessibility, and single-spa micro-frontends for shared authentication (including Google, Microsoft and Okta SSO) and Stripe checkout. Has 3+ years of Next.js experience, including a customer-facing booking platform that moved from the Pages Router to the App Router. Built custom MCP servers for SDK docs and Figma checks, set up Copilot first-pass code review, and wrote custom AI skills. Stood in as product owner for a couple of sprints, introduced a design, backend and frontend kickoff that later product owners kept, and mentored 5 or 6 interns and juniors. Now doing applied AI and full-stack work, with strengths across React, TypeScript, component architecture, micro-frontends, SDK authorship, LLM integration, and full-stack delivery.

experience.description: Software Engineer at SwiftConnect in Montréal, QC (Nov 2020 to Mar 2026), building enterprise access and security management SaaS with React, TypeScript, Next.js, React Native, Node.js, Ant Design, Styled Components, Redux Toolkit, Zustand, and TanStack Query. Built shared SDKs, a component library, single-spa micro-frontends, internal support tooling, observability, and AI-assisted engineering workflows.
highlights: Built the core access-control web client in React and TypeScript, with Redux Toolkit and TanStack Query handling complex authorization data so the UI stays stable during heavy mutations across multiple product areas.

Replaced copy-pasted API code in every project with one versioned Node.js SDK and a React SDK on top of it, published from a monorepo (pnpm workspaces, later Bun workspaces) to a private npm registry with semantic versions and a changelog. Almost the whole front-end team adopted them, and third-party customers integrated through the same SDKs.

Built a Storybook-documented component library from scratch, in its own repo with a standalone Webpack config, merging three projects' copies of the same UI into one and cutting duplicated UI code by roughly two thirds (estimate). A fourth app, moved from Angular 1.6 to React, used it from day one.

Built accessibility into the component library to WCAG AA, with keyboard navigation, focus management and colour contrast, tested with the Storybook a11y addon, jest-axe and screen reader checks, first in a Husky pre-commit hook and later in CI.
Set up single-spa micro-frontends from scratch and worked with them for 3+ years: a shared authentication app and a shared checkout app that the other web apps redirect to, deployed independently.

Integrated SSO sign-in with Google, Microsoft and Okta (OAuth, OIDC, SAML) in the shared auth app, and built the booking checkout on Stripe, styled to match the product, with card data staying with Stripe.

Built a customer-facing meeting-room booking platform in Next.js from scratch. It started on the Pages Router, moved to the App Router, and has run in production with real customers for more than 3 years, using API routes, server actions and middleware.

Replaced a daily forced logout with 15-minute access tokens that renew from a session token on user activity or focus, designed with a proof of concept and team feedback so customers stay signed in longer without weakening security.

Built service worker support for a web app (offline use, cached assets, FCM web push, background sync of CSV uploads) and moved CSV parsing of files up to 5 MB and other CPU-heavy work into Web Workers.

Added list and table virtualization to heavy tables, used memoization and React Profiler to stop unrelated re-renders, and moved the Create React App web apps to Vite with code splitting and tree-shaking, roughly halving the bundle (estimate).

Stopped big forms from re-rendering every field on each keystroke by giving each input its own Zustand subscription, a pattern the team adopted across most web and mobile projects, and moved UI state from Redux Toolkit to Zustand while keeping server data in TanStack Query.

Built, from scratch, an internal React Native (Expo) dashboard that lets customer support see failures and respond from company phones, with push notifications and React Native Testing Library coverage. CPU-heavy list work runs in background workers.
Replaced React Navigation with Expo's file-based router to cut Dependabot alerts and config overhead.
Delivered a React web dashboard error table and Slack alerts so support, ops and customer teams stopped contacting engineers to decode raw logs.
Cut email template turnaround from 3 to 4 days to hours or minutes by moving SendGrid templates into shared React components deployed by CI/CD.

Set up Sentry on the React Native app and then the web apps, with release tracking, source maps and alert routing, and tracked Core Web Vitals in production. Added event tracking with Google Analytics and then Mixpanel to see which features customers used.

Built a custom MCP server over the SDK docs and a custom Figma MCP with a design-contract check that cut design revision cycles by roughly 25 to 30% (estimate), connected Storybook's MCP and the GitHub MCP, and wrote custom AI skills that carry each project's patterns.

Added a GitHub Copilot first-pass review before human review, with the GitHub MCP pulling PR comments and status into the editor, reducing PR turnaround from about 2 to 3 days to about 1 to 1.5 days, roughly 50% (estimate).
Stood in as product owner for a couple of sprints, and introduced a kickoff where design, backend and frontend agree the API contract before building, which later product owners kept.
Owned code review and CI standards, wrote and reviewed RFCs, kept the architectural decision records, interviewed junior and intern candidates, and mentored 5 or 6 interns and juniors.
Raised a design problem with multiple emails and phone numbers, built a proof of concept with editable inputs, and shipped it after customer feedback raised the same issue.

experience.description: Worked collaboratively in a team of 4 to develop web applications using React, Material-UI for the frontend, and Express, Node, MongoDB, Cloudinary Image uploader, and JWT authentication for the backend.
highlights: Developed frontend with React and Material-UI, focusing on modular components and responsive design.
Built and integrated REST APIs using Node.js, Express, and MongoDB, including authentication and file uploads.
Implemented JWT authentication and secure user flows.
Participated in agile sprints, code reviews, and collaborative problem-solving.

experience.description: Junior Software Developer at Guiker in Montréal, building iOS and Android features with React Native (Expo), TypeScript and Jest, and contributing to the React and TypeScript rewrite of the web product, with some Node.js and Express routing and middleware. Used GitLab for repos and CI/CD.
highlights: Cut lease signing from up to a week of agent visits to 1 to 2 days by building the online lease flow and in-app landlord and tenant chat, which also helped support onboard customers faster.
Contributed to the React and TypeScript rewrite of the main web product with Material-UI, JSS, REST APIs and Jest test coverage.
Owned some Node.js and Express routing and middleware logic.
Built the 9-page lease form and fixed needless re-renders caused by React Context with memoization.
Built iOS and Android features in React Native (Expo) with TypeScript and Jest.

experience.description: Remote technical support and inbound sales for customers of four telecom and internet providers in the UK and Canada, over phone and remote desktop. Part-time until Jun 2018, then full-time until Jun 2019.
highlights: Ranked among the monthly top three agents throughout the tenure and received the monthly prize for it.

Supported customers of four telecom and internet providers in the UK and Canada over phone and remote desktop, working through many calls and several tickets a day, for customers from first-time computer users to experienced ones.
Fixed Windows and Mac problems: OS errors, corrupted installations, driver conflicts and application failures.
Walked customers through router setup, port forwarding and home network troubleshooting by phone, in steps a non-technical person could follow.
Fixed email problems across providers and clients: account setup, send and receive failures, access recovery, and sync on desktop and mobile.
Handled each case from start to finish: collected symptoms, reproduced the issue remotely, applied the fix, confirmed with the customer and documented the outcome before closing.
Spent the first roughly six months on inbound sales calls, qualifying customer needs and selling support packages, about 8 to 9 sales a month (estimate).

projects.title: Z-Graph: Interactive Math Visualization Platform
projects.excerpt: An interactive math visualization product built to explore equations, curves, fields, fractals, and surfaces across both 2D and 3D, with live formula editing and immediate visual feedback.
projects.shortDescription: Z-Graph is a graphics-heavy React and TypeScript application for exploring mathematical behavior visually instead of treating equations as static text. It combines Cartesian graphs, trigonometric and logarithmic functions, implicit curves, calculus visuals, polar and parametric systems, vector and slope fields, Fourier-style expressions, complex-plane visuals, fractals, parametric surfaces, and implicit 3D surfaces in one consistent interface. I structured it around reusable category definitions, configurable parameters, and worker-assisted computation so the app stays extensible and responsive as the rendering workload gets heavier.
highlights: Supports a wide range of graphing modes including algebra, calculus, polar, parametric, vector-field, fractal, and 3D surface exploration
Live formula editing, presets, parameter controls, animation, fullscreen mode, and PNG export turn equations into interactive systems
Reusable category-based architecture plus worker-assisted computation keeps graphics-heavy visualization maintainable and responsive

projects.title: ZTable: React Native Chemistry Reference App
projects.excerpt: A production-minded Expo and React Native chemistry app that combines a periodic table, localized element detail screens, atom-shell visualization, ion references, and classroom-oriented tools in a cleaner feature-based architecture.
projects.shortDescription: ZTable is a React Native chemistry reference and learning app built with Expo, TypeScript, Expo Router, Zustand, and NativeWind. The codebase was heavily refactored to move oversized TSX screens and chemistry utilities into feature-based modules, with thin route shells in `app/`, domain logic in `features/chemistry`, reusable UI in `components/`, and structured translations in `i18n/`. The result is a mobile app that stays readable, scalable, and maintainable while preserving public behavior across the periodic table, localized element profiles, atomic visualization, ion references, worksheets, and chemistry utilities.
highlights: Feature-based refactor split large route components, chemistry logic, and locale files into smaller focused modules
Periodic table, localized element details, atom visualization, ion references, worksheet tooling, and chemistry helpers live behind clearer reusable boundaries
Typecheck, lint, formatting, and Bun-based chemistry tests were stabilized so the refactor improved structure without regressing behavior

projects.title: Whisper Chat: Cross-Platform Real-Time Messaging App
projects.excerpt: A full-stack real-time messaging platform with Expo mobile, React web, and an Express plus Socket.IO backend, built to show production-style chat behavior instead of tutorial-level fake messaging.
projects.shortDescription: Whisper Chat is a full-stack TypeScript messaging system with three coordinated parts: a mobile client built with Expo and React Native, a web client built with React and Vite, and a backend API built with Express, Socket.IO, MongoDB, and Mongoose. It uses Clerk for authentication across web, mobile, and backend, TanStack Query for server state, Zustand for transient realtime state, and refactored socket modules for connection state, events, cache updates, unread markers, typing indicators, and online presence. The project focuses on real architecture: authenticated REST plus websocket flows, optimistic message sending, cross-platform product consistency, and maintainable state boundaries.
highlights: Shared backend supports authenticated REST APIs and authenticated websocket connections for both web and mobile clients
Realtime features include one-to-one chat creation, optimistic messaging, typing indicators, online presence, unread state, and chat preview updates
TanStack Query and Zustand are separated by responsibility so server state and realtime UI state stay maintainable as the app grows

projects.title: zsk-react-error: React Error Boundary & Reporter
projects.excerpt: A TypeScript-first React error boundary and reporter package with advanced error state control, reset logic, and analytics integration. Designed for scalable, production-grade error handling in React apps.
projects.shortDescription: A robust React error boundary and reporter package supporting both global and local error state, composable hooks, imperative resets, and flexible fallback UI. Integrates easily with Zustand and analytics tools for complete error visibility.
highlights: Global and local error state management with composable hooks
Keyed error isolation and imperative reset support
Customizable fallback UI and error reporting integration
Optimized for performance and scalable error handling
Easy integration with Zustand and analytics tools

projects.title: Smart AI: Full-Stack SaaS AI Platform
projects.excerpt: A comprehensive SaaS platform democratizing access to AI capabilities. Provides features for article generation, image creation/editing, resume analysis, and community interaction—with freemium tier distinction enforced at the API boundary.
projects.shortDescription: Full-stack AI-powered SaaS application integrating multiple AI services (Gemini, ClipDrop) and media processing (Cloudinary) with plan-based access control. Features user dashboards, creation history, community feed, and usage tracking.
highlights: Full-stack architecture with Express backend and React frontend
Integrated AI services: Google Gemini (text), ClipDrop (images), Cloudinary (storage)
Plan-based access control enforced server-side with Clerk authentication
User creation history, community feed, and like/publish system
Usage tracking and rate limiting for free tier users
MikroORM for type-safe database operations with PostgreSQL
Comprehensive API routes for AI generation and user management

projects.title: Auto Pause & Media Control: Chrome Extension
projects.excerpt: A zero-dependency Chrome extension that automatically pauses media when you switch tabs and gives you precise scroll-wheel control over volume, playback speed, and scrubbing—no library required, just clean browser APIs.
projects.shortDescription: A lightweight, privacy-first Chrome extension built on pure vanilla JavaScript and the Chrome Extensions API. It intelligently pauses audio/video on tab blur and resumes on return, with scroll-wheel shortcuts for volume, speed, and scrubbing. Includes a Glassmorphism popup UI with individual feature toggles and a master kill-switch.
highlights: Smart Auto-Pause: pauses media on tab switch and resumes precisely on return
Precision Media Scrubbing via Shift+Alt+Scroll using smooth trackpad scaling
Master Volume Control with Alt+Scroll hover gesture
Dynamic Playback Speed (0.25x–4.0x) via Ctrl+Alt+Scroll
Glassmorphism popup UI with per-feature toggles and a master power switch
Zero data collected—pure local JavaScript with no external dependencies

projects.title: zsk-portfolio: This Portfolio (over-engineered by design)
projects.excerpt: The site you're looking at right now. Built as a deliberate exercise in senior-level architecture using React 19, Vanilla Extract, Zustand, a zero-runtime CSS design system, and a focused AI resume assistant backed by FastAPI, Groq, and Redis rate limiting.
projects.shortDescription: A fully interactive developer portfolio built to showcase architectural decision-making as much as UI craft. Uses a headless JSON data layer, type-safe CSS-in-JS compiled at build time, compound component patterns, PWA offline support, a synthetic Web Audio click engine, hydration-safe state persistence, and an Ask AI experience. The AI feature connects the React frontend to a separate FastAPI backend that reads a structured resume profile JSON, calls Groq with a strict prompt, prioritizes professional experience before project evidence, caches repeated questions with Upstash Redis, and supports IP-based production rate limiting.
highlights: Added an Ask AI portfolio assistant with React chat UI, FastAPI backend, Groq Llama integration, strict prompt rules, and JSON-only responses
Implemented Upstash Redis caching and IP-based rate limiting, with local development bypass and production controls
Reduced LLM token usage by compacting the resume profile before each Groq request and versioning Redis cache keys when prompt behavior changes
Zero-runtime CSS via Vanilla Extract — styles are TypeScript, compiled to static .css at build time
15+ hot-swappable color themes built on a typed createThemeContract design system
React 19 Compiler integration — automatic memoization, no manual useMemo/useCallback
Headless JSON data layer in /public — fully decoupled from the UI, reusable across any future rebuild
Synthetic click sounds via Web Audio API (no .mp3 files, no network requests)
PWA-ready via vite-plugin-pwa with offline service worker caching
Keyboard accessibility: T (theme), M (mute), Cmd+D (download CV)
Custom NPM packages: zsk-react-error and zsk-react-i18n used in production

projects.title: zsk-use-sound: React Hook for File + Generated Sound
projects.excerpt: A TypeScript-first React hook inspired by use-sound that supports both Howler-powered file playback and browser-generated click sounds through one API. Designed for UI feedback without forcing bundled audio assets.
projects.shortDescription: zsk-use-sound unifies two sound strategies in one ergonomic hook: file mode for mp3/wav assets via Howler, and generated mode that synthesizes built-in click profiles in the browser when no file is provided. It exposes a familiar tuple API with play controls, mode visibility, and sound-enabled toggling for app-wide mute workflows.
highlights: Dual-mode audio engine: file playback (Howler) and generated Web Audio click presets
TypeScript-first API with exported option/play/control types for consumer safety
Built-in generated profiles (click, soft-click, tick) with volume and playback controls
Supports global mute flow via soundEnabled and per-play override via forceSoundEnabled
use-sound-inspired tuple return shape with stop, pause, duration, and runtime mode metadata

projects.title: zsk-jd: AI-Powered Resume Tailoring Skill
projects.excerpt: A Claude skill that runs ATS gap analysis and tailors a short, human-sounding resume to any job description from a master resume and an impact bank of real stories, with a mandatory trap scan, a gap check, and separate modes for technical support and product-angle resumes.
projects.shortDescription: A structured Claude skill that automates resume tailoring end to end: JD parsing, an AI-trap scan, skill gap scoring, a gap check against an impact bank of real stories, and compilable LaTeX output with optional cover letters. Built with strict ATS writing rules and truthfulness guardrails: every fact must come from the master resume, the bank, or the user's own answer.
highlights: Performs weighted skill gap analysis (hard skills 60%, seniority 25%, domain fit 15%) and reports a chance versus the user's usual instead of a numeric probability
Scans the job posting for hidden instructions aimed at AI tools and stops until the user confirms, so a trap can never shape the resume
Asks gap-check questions only about skills the master resume and the impact bank do not already answer, and never lets a bare yes put a skill on the resume
Builds a one-sentence summary and result-first bullets from bank stories, with Do not claim lines, estimate labels, and no invented numbers or titles
Separate modes for technical support (--TS) and a product angle (--PM), each with its own bank and title rules
Generates compilable LaTeX cover letters in 3 length modes (120, 200 and 350 words max) plus cover-only, with formal or casual tone flags
Patch mode outputs only changed LaTeX blocks for clean diffs in version control
Strict writing rules: banned AI-sounding words, no em dashes, no repeated bullet openers, no robotic summary openers
Written for Claude. Other LLM tools may read the skill but are untested

projects.title: Coin Gate: Live Crypto Market Dashboard
projects.excerpt: A production-style crypto dashboard built with Next.js 16, React 19, and TypeScript. It combines server-rendered CoinGecko market data with live websocket updates for pricing, trades, OHLC charts, search, and coin conversion in one responsive interface.
projects.shortDescription: Coin Gate is a crypto market dashboard built with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Base UI primitives, and lightweight-charts. It includes a home dashboard with featured market views, a paginated coins page, and dynamic coin detail screens with live pricing, recent trades, OHLC charting, and conversion tools. I used server components, client components, route handlers, and websocket subscriptions together so the app can load stable market snapshots first, then layer in live updates without losing responsiveness.
highlights: Home dashboard with featured coin overview, trending assets, and top categories
Paginated coins listing plus dynamic coin pages with live pricing, trades, OHLC charts, and conversion
Shared CoinGecko data layer handling REST, websocket streams, demo/pro API differences, and OHLC fallback logic

projects.title: zperiod: Interactive Chemistry Learning Web App
projects.excerpt: A modern React chemistry console with a searchable periodic table, element profiles, 3D atom visualization, molar mass calculation, equation balancing, ion references, solubility lookup, and worksheet PDF generation.
projects.shortDescription: zperiod is a browser-based chemistry learning app built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Bun, TanStack Router, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, vanilla-extract, React Three Fiber, Drei, Three.js, Framer Motion, Vitest, Testing Library, Web Workers, and zsk-react-i18n. It combines a searchable 118-element periodic table with category filters, detailed element profiles, isotope-aware atom visualization, molar mass parsing, equation balancing, common ion references, solubility lookup, and print-ready worksheet generation. The implementation separates pure chemistry logic from React UI, lazy-loads route screens, keeps equation balancing off the main thread, and uses several reasonable optimization techniques without overselling the app as fully optimized.
highlights: Interactive periodic table with search, category filtering, detailed element profiles, common ion data, and localized English/French content
Chemistry tools include molar mass calculation, equation balancing with exact fraction math in a Web Worker, solubility lookup, and worksheet PDF generation
3D atom model uses React Three Fiber, Drei, Three.js, memoized shell helpers, and lazy loading so heavy visual features stay outside the startup path

projects.title: Z Gym: Premium Fitness Brand SPA
projects.excerpt: A production-style fitness SPA built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, and Motion. I treated it like a real frontend system, with scroll-driven sections, reusable UI primitives, typed content, and theme support instead of one-off page styling.
projects.shortDescription: Z Gym is a premium fitness brand experience built as a section-based single-page app. It uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI primitives, and Motion for scroll-driven storytelling, responsive layout, and polished dark and light themes. For me, this project is a good example of building more than a modern-looking website. It is also structured to be scalable, reusable, and maintainable, with isolated section components, reusable hooks, shared animation variants, direct imports, and a centralized typed content layer that keeps the codebase held to a high standard.
highlights: Scroll-driven single-page experience with responsive section architecture and premium visual pacing
Reusable UI primitives, shared animation variants, and isolated section components instead of page-specific one-offs
Centralized typed content plus theme support and accessible interactions built for maintainability, not only presentation

projects.title: WC26: Open-Source World Cup 2026 macOS Menu Bar App
projects.excerpt: A small open-source macOS menu bar app built in SwiftUI to track World Cup 2026 fixtures, standings, and live scores without repeatedly opening a website or paying for a seasonal score app.
projects.shortDescription: WC26 is a practical native macOS side project I built as my first real Swift and SwiftUI app. I came into it from a senior frontend and full-stack background in React and TypeScript, using the project as a way to learn native app structure by shipping something genuinely useful for myself during the tournament season. The app runs from the menu bar using MenuBarExtra, fetches match data from the open-source `worldcup2026` API by Reza Rahiminia, normalizes raw match payloads into UI-friendly models, keeps live matches at the top, preserves stoppage-time formatting like 90'+8', and supports favorites, pinned live matches, notifications, refresh controls, start at login, and local preference persistence. It is intentionally small in scope, open source, and distributed unsigned because I did not want to pay the Apple developer fee for a fun side project.
highlights: Built as a native SwiftUI menu bar utility with fixtures, standings, team sheets, favorites, and live scores available in one click
Added a central AppViewModel, match normalization layer, and live-first ordering so messy API data becomes a cleaner real-time product experience
Improved timer parsing and notification handling to support meaningful details such as stoppage time, kickoff, goal, and full-time events
Stored user preferences locally for pinned matches, refresh interval, transparency, favorites, and notification behavior
Open-source project that credits the `worldcup2026` API provider directly and ships with honest unsigned-distribution tradeoffs

projects.title: Portfolio Ask AI
projects.excerpt: An end-to-end Ask AI portfolio feature with React 19, FastAPI, LLM inference, Redis caching, IP rate limiting, and structured resume-grounded answers.
projects.shortDescription: End-to-end Ask AI feature for izsk.dev with a FastAPI backend, LLM inference, Upstash Redis caching, IP rate limiting, and a structured prompt pipeline. The React 19 frontend handles cold-start wakeup, typed responses, source dropdowns, auto-growing input, keyboard shortcuts, and backend error surfacing.
highlights: Built a FastAPI backend integrating LLM inference APIs, structured prompt controls, JSON-only output, and resume-grounded answer rules
Used Upstash Redis for repeated-question caching, versioned cache keys, and IP-based production rate limiting at 3 requests per IP per hour
Shipped a React 19, TypeScript, and Vite chat frontend with cold-start wakeup, typed responses, source dropdowns, auto-growing input, and keyboard shortcuts
Surfaced backend and provider errors in the frontend so users see actionable states instead of generic failures

projects.title: Tubewise: YouTube Playlists Turned Into Courses
projects.excerpt: Turns any YouTube video or playlist into a structured course you actually finish: AI-written notes, practice problems, quizzes and a daily route drawn as metro stops.
projects.shortDescription: Tubewise turns a YouTube video or playlist into a course. Each video becomes a lesson with timestamped notes, easy/medium/hard practice problems (real LeetCode/GFG problems for DSA courses) and a quiz, and a wrong answer jumps the video to the moment that explains it. Notes are written by an AI coding agent from each video's own transcript through a custom MCP server and checked by server-side code before they are saved. Solo project, designed, built and deployed end to end on free tiers.
highlights: Live library of 4 courses and 206 lessons, 171 with AI-written notes; about 7,000 lines of TypeScript, 32 API route files and a custom MCP server with 8 tools

YouTube blocks caption downloads from cloud servers (5 of 5 requests failed from Vercel, while the same video returned 675 caption lines from a home connection), so the site stores metadata and my Mac downloads transcripts and uploads them through a token-scoped agent API

Server-side quality gate for AI notes after an early run produced 37 lessons from one template: timestamps must match real transcript lines, quiz options can't be copied from the summary, sentences can't repeat across lessons, and the longest option can't usually be the right answer

Authentication without an auth library: argon2id passwords with lockout, 15-minute JWT access tokens in httpOnly cookies, hashed refresh tokens rotated on every use, and reuse of an old token revokes every session; verified with 13 scripted scenarios
Safe AI write access to production: personal agent tokens (shown once, stored hashed, revocable) and a scoped agent API with no delete routes, with the same quality gate applied to agent saves
Moved from SQLite to Postgres by rewriting about 54 synchronous call sites as async, adding 5 versioned migrations and copying every row with its original id
Backups every 15 minutes (14 days kept), nightly off-site dumps, a read-only mirror the UI can switch to, and a 7-day trash for deleted courses
Runs entirely on free tiers (Vercel Hobby, Neon free); the only paid feature, an AI tutor, is optional and capped

Architecture: Next.js 16 (App Router) on Vercel, Postgres on Neon via drizzle-orm and node-postgres, React 19, antd 6 and TanStack Query; a custom MCP server on my Mac (stdio) lets Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Codex read lessons, upload transcripts and save notes through the agent API (9 of 32 API route files)
Public read, private write: anyone can browse, every write is owner-only on the server, the UI hides controls that would fail, and internal error details never reach the browser
Lessons are laid out as a daily route (30-120 min/day) drawn as metro stops; videos with chapters are split per chapter and playlists are checked daily for new videos

Next: scope every query by user id for more than one owner, add a cloud option for fetching transcripts, and enable the AI tutor (Claude Haiku with prompt caching and daily caps) on the live site once usage justifies the cost

Breaks down Axios security incidents and supply-chain risk as a decision factor
Explains why Ky became the default request layer for modern React projects

blog.title: Context vs Redux Toolkit vs Zustand: Picking the Right State Tool for the Job

highlights: Maps the strengths and weaknesses of Context, Redux Toolkit, and Zustand
Explains the Context re-render trap and why selector-based stores feel better at scale
Shows when scoped Zustand plus Context is the right hybrid pattern

blog.title: React Query vs SWR vs the `use` Hook: Why You're Fetching Data Wrong
blog.excerpt: You already know how to fetch data. What you're missing is everything that happens after.
blog.shortDescription: A production-focused comparison of raw fetch, SWR, React 19's `use` hook, and TanStack Query, centered on caching, mutations, race conditions, and why client-side data fetching is really a state synchronization problem.
highlights: Explains where raw fetch and Axios break down once caching, deduplication, and stale data enter the picture
Shows why the React 19 `use` hook is powerful in server components but limited as a client-side data fetching strategy
Compares SWR and TanStack Query through mutations, optimistic updates, DevTools, infinite queries, and real production tradeoffs

blog.title: You're Probably Using React Memoization Wrong (And So Was I)
blog.excerpt: Memoization is a performance tool, not a coding habit. Most of the time, the simpler version is the better version.
blog.shortDescription: A practical guide to `useMemo`, `useCallback`, and `React.memo`, focused on when they solve real performance problems, when they add noise, and how React 19 changes the tradeoffs.
highlights: Explains when `useMemo`, `useCallback`, and `React.memo` actually save meaningful work
Breaks down the reference equality traps that make manual memoization ineffective
Shows how React 19, `useDeferredValue`, and `useTransition` shift the performance conversation beyond blanket memoization

blog.title: React Compound Components: The Pattern That Makes Component APIs Actually Good

blog.shortDescription: A practical deep dive into the compound components pattern in React, covering why monolithic prop-driven APIs become unmaintainable, how Context-based composition gives consumers layout control without losing shared state, and how to design the pattern correctly in TypeScript for real component libraries and design systems.

Explains controlled vs uncontrolled APIs, namespaced TypeScript sub-components, and why Context beats `React.Children.map` here

blog.title: React Virtualization: Fast Tables With Thousands of Rows
blog.excerpt: A practical, opinionated deep dive into React list and table virtualization focused on large datasets, real bottlenecks, and the tradeoffs behind adding windowing at all.
blog.shortDescription: This article treats virtualization as a DOM scaling problem first and a React implementation detail second. It starts with a DevTools-based workflow to confirm whether rendering cost is actually the bottleneck before reaching for a library, then walks through how windowing works under the hood, when it is the right call, when it is unnecessary, and how to implement it with TanStack Virtual, react-window, react-virtuoso, TanStack Table, and TanStack Query. highlights: Explains virtualization from first principles: DOM recycling, scroll math, overscan, and why the browser usually fails before React does
Shows when to use virtualization and when to skip it for simpler options such as pagination, server-side filtering, or append-only lists
Includes practical implementations with TanStack Virtual, react-window, react-virtuoso, TanStack Table, and `useInfiniteQuery`
Covers variable-height rows, sticky header setup, refetch scroll-loss issues, and other failure modes that appear in real tables
Ends with the same rule as the rest of the series: measure first, then add complexity only when the evidence says you need it

blog.title: Concurrent Rendering in React: What It Actually Is, And When It's Just Hiding a Problem
blog.excerpt: Concurrent rendering is not multi-threading. It's React's way of rescheduling render work so urgent updates stay responsive.
blog.shortDescription: A technical deep dive into React's concurrent rendering model, focused on what Fiber actually enables, how urgent and non-urgent updates shape the API surface, when `startTransition`, `useTransition`, and `useDeferredValue` genuinely help, and when they are just masking a slower underlying problem.

Breaks down `startTransition`, `useTransition`, and `useDeferredValue` through real UI cases and a clear decision table
Shows how concurrent rendering and Suspense fit together in data-heavy flows such as product detail navigation
Ends with a practical diagnosis framework so you measure the real bottleneck before reaching for any concurrent API

blog.title: React Reconciliation and Keys: What's Actually Happening When Your Component Re-Renders
blog.excerpt: Keys do not magically fix list bugs. They tell React which child identity should survive the next diff.

Shows step by step why removing an item from a stateful list breaks under positional diffing and why index keys behave the same way
Clarifies the exact difference between a re-render and a remount, including what state survives and what resets
Connects reconciliation to Fiber internals, current versus work-in-progress trees, and practical DevTools debugging for unexpected remounts

blog.title: JavaScript Loops: Stop Using map() for Everything

Explains the real tradeoffs behind `for`, `for...of`, `forEach`, `map`, `filter`, and `reduce` instead of treating them as style preferences

blog.title: Debugging React Apps Like a Senior Dev

Covers the highest-frequency React bug classes including unstable effect dependencies, stale closures, render storms, cache confusion, and memory leaks
Includes practical production debugging guidance for source maps in Vite, Sentry with React error boundaries, feature flags, and structured console breadcrumbs

blog.title: Web Performance Beyond Lighthouse: What Actually Moves the Needle

Covers WebSocket ticket authentication, ping/pong heartbeats, jittered exponential backoff, and Redis pub/sub fan-out

blog.title: Server State vs Real-Time State: Stop Putting Both in One Store

Builds one socket module outside React that calls `setQueryData` when the event carries the full entity and `invalidateQueries` when it only signals change

blog.title: Monorepo vs Polyrepo for Small Teams: Why I Pick Monorepo

blog.title: FlashList vs FlatList: Stop Shipping FlatList for Real Feeds
